name: Wasserman (now THE·TEAM)
status: Renamed THE·TEAM in March 2026 and now fully owned by the investment firm Providence Equity. Founder Casey Wasserman has sold out but is still chairperson of the LA 2028 Olympics. Its baseball agent Joel Wolfe represents most of the top Japanese pitchers in MLB.
summary: A Los Angeles sports and entertainment agency founded in 2002. It became the main American agency for Japanese baseball stars (Darvish, Senga, Seiya Suzuki, Yamamoto, Sasaki) through one American agent, Joel Wolfe, building on the door first opened by Arn Tellem and Don Nomura. In 2026 the founder was forced out after his name appeared in the Epstein files, and the company changed its name.
quick_facts: 2002 in Los Angeles by Casey Wasserman, grandson of Hollywood executive Lew Wasserman
Wasserman Media Group (2002) → Wasserman (2016) → THE·TEAM (9 March 2026)
Providence Equity Partners, an investment firm. It first invested in 2022 (terms not disclosed), was reported to hold about 60% by 2026, and bought out the founder on 5 Oct 2026
Mike Watts, with the company since 2002 and president since 2014; CEO since the buyout closed on 5 Oct 2026
About $3.4 billion (REPORTED by Sportico and Puck from unnamed sources, July 2026; the price was never made official)

No. 2 sports agency in the world in Forbes' 2025 ranking, behind CAA: over $9 billion in playing contracts, 4,000+ clients, offices in 28 countries (figures as relayed by The Big Lead and the company)
Joel Wolfe, executive vice president, baseball
Yu Darvish, Kodai Senga, Seiya Suzuki, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Roki Sasaki, Yoshitomo Tsutsugo; in basketball, Rui Hachimura

sections.title: In short
sections.intro: Your three questions, answered briefly. (1) Japanese agent: I found no named Japanese agent inside the firm. The face is an American, Joel Wolfe; the Japanese side comes from partners in Japan. (2) Business model: it earns a percentage of player contracts and sponsor deals, and it grew by buying other agencies with investor money. (3) LA Olympics: the link is personal, not corporate. Founder Casey Wasserman chairs LA28, but since 2026 he no longer owns the agency. (4) Negotiation: its trademark is the opt-out and other protections for the player, plus a tightly run, equal-rules bidding process. See chapter 6.

cells: Casey Wasserman founds Wasserman Media Group.
Buys agent Arn Tellem's basketball and baseball business. Tellem had worked with Don Nomura on Hideo Nomo in 1995, so the Japan know-how arrives with him.
Yu Darvish is represented by 'Arn Tellem of Wasserman Media Group and Don Nomura'; signs with Texas.
Tellem leaves for the Detroit Pistons. Kenta Maeda hires Wasserman's Adam Katz.
Buys the music business of the Paradigm agency and starts Wasserman Music.
Providence Equity invests (terms not disclosed) and buys out two earlier investors. Casey Wasserman keeps control at this point; by 2026 Providence is reported to hold about 60%.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto picks Joel Wolfe; he later signs with the Dodgers for 12 years and $325 million.
Roki Sasaki picks Wolfe. Team meetings are held at Wasserman's Los Angeles office.

30 Jan: the US Justice Department releases Epstein-related files that include 2003 emails between Casey Wasserman and Ghislaine Maxwell. Clients start leaving. 13 Feb: he says he will sell and step back.
Providence confirms it will buy the founder's remaining stake.
Buyout completed on 5 Oct; Mike Watts becomes CEO. On 10 Nov a new 11-member board is announced. It includes Jason Ranne, one of Rui Hachimura's agents. Price not disclosed.

sections.title: Japanese athletes it represents
sections.intro: Client lists change, so read every row as 'reported at that date'.

cells: With the firm since 2011–12 (first through Tellem with Nomura, later Joel Wolfe). Baseball-Reference lists his agents as THE·TEAM.
Hired Wasserman's Adam Katz for his 2015 move.
Kodai Senga, Seiya Suzuki, Yoshitomo Tsutsugo
Named as Wolfe clients by Daily Sports (Nov 2024).
MLB's Japanese site names Wolfe as his agent in its winter-meetings preview.
American with a Japanese mother; played for Japan at the 2023 WBC. Wolfe travelled with him on a promotional tour of Japan.
Signed with the firm in Nov 2021. Tokyo Sports framed it around the record Darvish and Maeda trusted, and said Wolfe had earlier worked under Tellem supporting Hideki Matsui.
Signed in May 2019. His agents are Jason Ranne and Darren Matsubara. He said he chose them himself.
Kawamura signed on 29 Jun 2023; the same report lists Watanabe as a client.

rows: No named Japanese agent inside the firm was found, and no Tokyo office or Japan company (two separate searches, 21 Nov 2026). Every report names Americans: Joel Wolfe in baseball, Jason Ranne and Darren Matsubara in basketball.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/841690
One Japanese-speaking staff member is named: Mako Allbee, described as from the Wasserman office, interpreted at Yamamoto's Dodgers press conference. Her job title was not found (headline only).
https://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/828990
Stage 1 (1995–2015): the Japanese side was an outside partner. Don Nomura had the player's trust; Tellem had the American firm. See Don Nomura's page.
https://www.mlbtraderumors.com/2011/10/agents-predict-darvish-posting-fee-contract.html

Stage 2 (today): the Japanese side is a management company in Japan. US media say the high-school pitcher Shoki Oda belongs to 'the same Japanese management company' that helped Yamamoto and Sasaki move.
https://www.tokyo-sports.co.jp/articles/-/409655

Which company? No on-the-record source names it. One web outlet (Sirabee, April 2024, anonymous source) says it is the advertising giant Dentsu, that Dentsu manages Yamamoto and Sasaki, and that Dentsu preferred this agency for business reasons. Treat this as an unconfirmed claim.
No player has said in public who introduced him to Wolfe. A June 2024 US report says Sasaki was already getting guidance from Yamamoto's agent months before he signed.
https://dodgerblue.com/dodgers-rumors-roki-sasaki-receiving-guidance-from-yoshinobu-yamamotos-agent/2024/06/11/?noamp=mobile
So the pattern is two layers: a Japanese company looks after the player at home (ads, media, daily support) and the American agent negotiates with MLB clubs.

sections.title: How it wins Japanese players
sections.intro: These are the methods that show up in reports. The grouping is my analysis.

rows: A chain of clients. Each star makes the next one easier: Darvish, then Maeda, Senga, Suzuki, Yamamoto, Sasaki. Japanese papers introduce Wolfe by listing his Japanese clients.
https://www.daily.co.jp/mlb/2024/11/11/0018328136.shtml
Being seen in Japan. Wolfe went to Japan with his client Lars Nootbaar on a promotional tour and met people around Yamamoto.
https://www.mlb.com/news/lars-nootbaar-s-connection-with-yoshinobu-yamamoto
Running the process for the player. For Sasaki, about 20 clubs showed interest; meetings were held at the firm's Los Angeles office and limited to two hours each.
https://www.espn.com/mlb/story/_/id/43229907/roki-sasaki-agent-gives-update-recruiting-process-next-phase-expected-decision-line
Working with a partner in Japan instead of competing with it (Nomura then, a management company now).
https://www.tokyo-sports.co.jp/articles/-/409655
Los Angeles as a base: the office, the Dodgers, and a large Japanese community are all in one city.
https://www.postguam.com/sports/nation/paint-japan-blue-how-the-dodgers-vision-of-japanese-prominence-became-reality/article_f8d37448-039f-11f0-9e18-dfb70fdb6fe9.html

sections.title: Negotiation skills: seven case studies
sections.intro: What the firm's agents actually won, and where they could not. Contract terms are from AP, MLB.com, ESPN and MLB Trade Rumors. 'Opt-out' means the player may end the contract early and sell himself again. 'Posting fee' is the money the American club pays the Japanese club.

cells: Yoshinobu Yamamoto → Dodgers, Dec 2023. 12 years, $325 million (OFFICIAL terms via AP)

Record guarantee for a pitcher at the time. $50 million signing bonus, low pay in the first years. Two opt-outs (the right to leave early), with timing pushed back if his elbow is badly hurt. No no-trade clause, but if he is traded he may opt out. Interpreter, trainer, therapist and five return flights a year are written in. The Dodgers also paid Orix a $50.6 million posting fee.

Several clubs bid at the same level: the Mets reportedly offered the same $325 million and the Yankees $300 million over 10 years. The player then chose on fit, with no final round of raises reported.
The yearly average ($27 million) is lower than the Yankees' offer; length and total were put first. How Wolfe ran the meetings was not found.
Roki Sasaki → Dodgers, Jan 2025. Minor-league contract, $6.5 million bonus
He was under 25, so the rules capped his money: clubs could only pay from a small bonus pool (about $4 million to $7.5 million).

With price fixed, the agent built a contest on everything else. 20 clubs sent presentations, 8 got meetings at the firm's Los Angeles office, 3 became finalists. Every meeting had the same length (under two hours), no current players in the room, and the same 'homework assignment' for each club.

Rival clubs suspected a pre-arranged Dodgers deal and complained; MLB looked into it and found no evidence. Wolfe denied it strongly and called the final choice close to a coin flip. Some clubs disliked handing over their own analysis for little chance.
Kodai Senga → Mets, Dec 2022. 5 years, $75 million
Opt-out after 2025 only if he pitched 400 innings. Full no-trade for three years. In return the Mets got a cheap extra year if his elbow needed major surgery. Bonuses for Cy Young award votes.
A swap of risks: the club's worry about the elbow was answered with conditions, not with less money.
Wolfe's own part in the talks is not described in reports.
Seiya Suzuki → Cubs, Mar 2022. 5 years, $85 million
Full no-trade clause. Then a record for a Japanese position player. Cubs also paid Hiroshima a $14.6 million posting fee.
Time pressure handled: the 99-day MLB lockout froze his 30-day window, leaving about 20 days to finish.
Which clubs made formal offers is not stated.
Yu Darvish → Rangers, Jan 2012. About 6 years, $60 million (Tellem with Don Nomura)
A clause let him leave a year early if he reached high Cy Young award results. Rangers paid Nippon-Ham a record $51.7 million posting fee.
Signed at the very last hour of the 30-day window. Both sides had something to lose: he would have gone back to Japan, and Texas would have lost its chance.
Yu Darvish → Padres extension, Feb 2023. 6 years, $108 million
Signed at age 36, runs to 42, full no-trade.
Security over yearly pay: a lower yearly average helped the club's tax bill, and he got six guaranteed years.
Which agent led the talks is not confirmed.
Kenta Maeda → Dodgers, Jan 2016. 8 years, only $25 million guaranteed
Bonuses could lift it above $100 million. No opt-out. Dodgers paid Hiroshima a $20 million posting fee.
The example of weak bargaining power: a medical exam found elbow problems, few clubs stayed in, and the old rules capped the fee at $20 million.
Widely called a club-friendly deal. One column said it pushed the injury risk onto the player and blamed the posting rules more than the agent.

parts.heading: Nine techniques that repeat (my analysis)
rows: 1. Opt-outs. Almost every deal has an exit so the player can go back to the market if he does better than expected (Yamamoto, Senga, Darvish).
https://www.foxsports.com/articles/mlb/yamamotos-contract-with-dodgers-includes-2-opt-outs-but-timing-depends-on-elbow-health
2. Trade health risk for conditions, not for less money. When a club fears an elbow injury, tie the opt-out date or an extra club year to that injury (Yamamoto, Senga).
https://www.thescore.com/mlb/news/2519573
3. Protection from being moved: a no-trade clause, or 'if you trade me I can leave' when the club refuses one (Suzuki, Senga, Darvish, Yamamoto).
https://www.foxsports.com/articles/mlb/yamamotos-contract-with-dodgers-includes-2-opt-outs-but-timing-depends-on-elbow-health
4. Cash early: big signing bonus, low first-year pay. The player gets money early and for certain; the club gets an easier budget (Yamamoto's $50 million bonus).
https://www.foxsports.com/articles/mlb/yamamotos-contract-with-dodgers-includes-2-opt-outs-but-timing-depends-on-elbow-health
5. Equal rules for every bidder: same meeting length, same assignment, one neutral place. This creates a contest even when price is fixed, and it is a defence if someone cries foul (Sasaki).
https://www.mlb.com/news/roki-sasaki-s-agent-discusses-meetings-mlb-teams
6. Use the calendar. Posting windows force clubs to decide (Darvish 2012 at the final hour; Suzuki after the lockout).
https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/darvish-rangers-agree-to-60m-6-yr-deadline-deal
7. Gather several top bids, then let the player pick on fit (Yamamoto).
https://www.mlbtraderumors.com/2023/12/latest-on-yankees-mets-failed-pursuits-of-yoshinobu-yamamoto.html
8. Write daily life into the contract for Japanese players: interpreter, trainer, therapist, flights home, no demotion without consent (Yamamoto, Senga).
https://www.foxsports.com/articles/mlb/yamamotos-contract-with-dodgers-includes-2-opt-outs-but-timing-depends-on-elbow-health
9. Speak in public. Wolfe holds on-record briefings, explains the process, and answers accusations directly (Sasaki).
https://www.si.com/mlb/diamondbacks/arizona-diamondbacks-news/q-a-with-roki-sasaki-s-agent-joel-wolfe-winter-meetings

parts.heading: Where even a good agent has little power
rows: When rules cap the money. For Sasaki, Wolfe said the differences between clubs' bonus pools were tiny and told him not to choose on them.
https://www.si.com/mlb/diamondbacks/arizona-diamondbacks-news/q-a-with-roki-sasaki-s-agent-joel-wolfe-winter-meetings
When only one club is willing. Maeda in 2016: one report says the Dodgers may have been the only club ready to pay the posting fee.
https://sports.vice.com/en/article/bmq8j3/kenta-maedas-contract-is-bad-news-for-baseball-players
When the market is slow. Darvish in 2018 reportedly hoped for $155–175 million and signed for $126 million.
https://www.mlbtraderumors.com/2018/02/reactions-to-and-effects-of-the-yu-darvish-deal.html
Suspicion is a cost too. The Dodgers had kept $2.5 million of bonus money unspent before Sasaki, which fed the talk of a fixed deal.
https://www.tsn.ca/mlb/mlb-investigated-to-ensure-no-early-roki-sasaki-deal-in-place-1.2218035

parts.heading: Who is Joel Wolfe?
rows: Title: Executive Vice President and Managing Executive, Baseball. He leads the baseball group together with B.B. Abbott.
https://www.teamwass.com/?p=19211

Background (REPORTED): a stats database lists a Joel Wolfe born 1970, from Los Angeles and UCLA, who played outfield in the minor leagues from 1991 to 1996 without reaching the majors. No article I read ties the two together, so treat it as likely, not confirmed.
https://www.statscrew.com/minorbaseball/stats/p-6788b321
He learned the Japan side under Arn Tellem, supporting Hideki Matsui, according to Tokyo Sports.
https://www.tokyo-sports.co.jp/articles/-/126297
His advice to young players: career earnings come from the long run, not the first bonus.
https://www.si.com/mlb/diamondbacks/arizona-diamondbacks-news/q-a-with-roki-sasaki-s-agent-joel-wolfe-winter-meetings
He also speaks for the player's situation at home. He said Sasaki was heavily criticised in Japan for leaving young.
https://www.si.com/mlb/diamondbacks/arizona-diamondbacks-news/q-a-with-roki-sasaki-s-agent-joel-wolfe-winter-meetings
Controversies about him personally, beyond the Sasaki accusations: none found (searched 21 Nov 2026).

sections.title: Why do Japanese baseball players choose one agency over another?
sections.intro: No player has explained his choice in public, so the ranking below is my analysis of the evidence. Short answer: pitchers follow the chain of earlier pitchers; hitters go to the agent who controls the market for hitters; and a company in Japan may be guiding the choice.

cells: When Yamamoto and Sasaki chose Joel Wolfe, Japanese papers introduced him by listing Darvish, Senga and Suzuki. Murakami's agent was introduced the same way: 'the man who worked with Masahiro Tanaka'.
Whoever already has a Japanese star
2. The agent's power in your part of the market
Murakami's agent Casey Close also represented the two biggest left-handed hitters on sale that winter (Schwarber and Tucker). Japanese papers said this let him steer which club went for which hitter.
Excel and Boras for hitters; Wasserman for pitchers
3. The company looking after you in Japan
Reports with anonymous sources say Dentsu manages Yamamoto and Sasaki at home and preferred Wasserman. Not confirmed.
A Japanese weekly credits Wasserman's staff support for players and families. Contracts include interpreters, trainers and flights home.
Shota Imanaga's agent is Yoshinori Hasegawa of Octagon, a Japanese agent certified by the MLB players' union since 2008.

Murakami signed with Close in September 2024, more than a year before his move. Sasaki was reported to be getting guidance from Yamamoto's agent months before he signed. The agent who arrives first often wins.
Yankees, 7 years, $155 million, with an opt-out and a full no-trade clause
Close kept the bids secret and, by one account, told clubs the floor was 6 years and $120 million. Excel has had its own Japanese track record since then.
White Sox, 2 years, $34 million; Yakult received a $6.575 million posting fee
Clubs worried about his strikeouts, so the big long deal did not come. Close took a short deal so Murakami can sell himself again at 27.
The other big hitter went to the other big hitters' agent. Papers described Close and Boras as splitting the infield market between them.
A Japanese agent inside an American firm can win a top pitcher. He joined through a small agency that Octagon bought in 2008.

parts.heading: So why Murakami with Excel and not Wasserman? (my reading)
rows: He is a hitter. Wasserman's Japanese strength is pitchers; sharing an agent with Yamamoto does nothing for a slugger's price.
https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/b287e01f5dd20428d8104e8d16858092e5ad2cae
Close had the Tanaka deal, the largest ever for a Japanese player at the time, plus Akiyama. That is a chain of his own.
https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/cfdca24703bb8e6880e4f67f388e8b0530eee841
Close held the other top left-handed hitters that winter, which gave him a view of every club's plans.
https://news.jsports.co.jp/baseball/article/20190310238385/
Not found: Murakami's own explanation, or which company manages him in Japan.

sections.title: Could a Japanese agency step into this field? (my analysis)
sections.intro: Honest view first: a small Japanese agency is unlikely to beat the American firms head-on at negotiating MLB contracts. But there are real openings, and Japanese companies are already taking some of them. The points below are my analysis, built on the cases on this site.

parts.heading: The entry rules
rows: Only an agent certified by the MLB players' union may negotiate an MLB contract. To be certified you apply (fee $2,500), pass a background check and a written exam, and must be named by at least one player.
https://www.agent.mlbplayers.com/application-instructions
Even recruiting players for a certified agent needs a limited certificate.
https://www.agent.mlbplayers.com/faqs
In Japan, a magazine report notes that only lawyers may act as agents in negotiations with Japanese clubs, so a Japanese agency needs lawyers for the home side.
https://smart-flash.jp/sports/76744/

cells: The player's trust, family, sponsors and media are in Japan. Reported fees are about 20% on sponsor deals against 4–5% on salary, so the home side is also where a Japanese firm can earn most.
Dentsu (reported) with Yamamoto and Sasaki; Hakuhodo buying Nomura's agency
2. Partner, but put it in writing
A formal co-agent role with an American firm gives the bargaining muscle without building it. The danger is being dropped once the American firm knows the player.
Nomura and Tellem on Darvish (2012); the bridge ended when Tellem left
3. Get one certified Japanese agent of your own
One person with the union certificate changes you from a helper into a negotiator.
Yoshinori Hasegawa at Octagon, certified since 2008
Relationships formed in high school or early in a Japanese career decide later choices. Players under 25 are capped on money, so fit and trust matter more than price.
Sasaki managed 'since high school' (reported); the 2026 race for Shoki Oda
Pitchers are taken. Hitters, relief pitchers, players coming back to Japan, and foreign players going to Japan are less crowded.
Nomura represented foreign players joining Japanese clubs
Interpreter, housing, family, training and life after baseball are things a Japanese firm does naturally.
Yamamoto's contract writes in an interpreter, trainer and flights
Taking money from a sponsor while representing the player can destroy trust.
The reported 2017 split between Darvish and Nomura
8. Do not depend on one person
Clients follow people. Train a second agent and sign clients to the firm.
Wasserman's own risk if Joel Wolfe ever left
Scale needs capital. Japanese advertising and entertainment companies are the natural backers.
Amuse (2019) and Hakuhodo (2025) with Nomura's agency

parts.heading: Who is most likely to succeed?
rows: Most likely: a big Japanese advertising or entertainment company that controls the home side and either employs or partners with one certified agent. This is already happening.
https://www.hakuhodo.co.jp/news/newsrelease/118591/
Possible: a small private agency that picks one gap (for example hitters, or high-school players heading to American colleges) and signs a written partnership with an American firm.
Least likely: a small agency trying to negotiate nine-figure MLB contracts alone, without a certified agent or a track record. Players choose proof, and the proof is past deals.

Commissions: the agency keeps a percentage of each playing contract it negotiates. Forbes' 2025 ranking (as relayed by The Big Lead) puts its maximum possible commissions at about $956 million, on more than $9 billion of playing contracts and nearly $2 billion of sponsor deals.
https://www.thebiglead.com/?p=109273
Rates (REPORTED): a Japanese weekly, quoting an unnamed MLB scout, puts its fee at about 4–5% of salary on team contracts and about 20% on sponsor deals. Not confirmed by the firm.
https://gendai.media/articles/-/116998?page=2
Service: the same report credits its staff's close support for players and their families as a reason Japanese players choose it.
https://gendai.media/articles/-/116998?page=2
Marketing: sponsor and advertising deals for athletes, plus consulting for brands. It calls itself a marketing and talent management company.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasserman_(company)

Growth by buying: more than 20 agencies since 2004, including Arn Tellem's practice (2006), a UK soccer agency (2006), Paradigm's live-music business (2021), the baseball agency Jet Sports (2022), Brillstein talent management (2023), hockey and football agencies (2024–25) and a golf agency (2026). List from Wikipedia.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasserman_(company)
Outside money: Providence Equity has owned most of it since 2022 and all of it since 2026. Investment firms also bought rivals (Goldman Sachs bought Excel).
https://www.sportico.com/business/finance/2026/providence-equity-wasserman-agency-sale-billion-1234940141/
Typical rates in the industry, for scale: 3% on NFL team contracts (the union maximum) and roughly 10–20% on sponsor deals, which unions do not regulate.
https://frontofficesports.com/article/how-much-do-nfl-agents-make/
It is much more than a sports agency now: music booking, brand consulting, talent management, broadcasters, speakers and online creators.
https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/providence-set-to-fully-acquire-casey-wassermans-theteam-valuing-agency-at-3-4b-report/

parts.heading: The biggest sports agencies (Forbes 2025, maximum commissions)

cells: About $20 billion in contracts. Represents Shohei Ohtani.
Goldman Sachs bought a majority in late 2025. Represents Munetaka Murakami.
Baseball only. Represents Kazuma Okamoto and Yusei Kikuchi.

parts.heading: Who represents the Japanese stars? 5 of the 9 I could source are with this agency

sections.title: The 2026 crisis
sections.intro: Facts as reported. No view is taken here on the people involved.

rows: 30 Jan 2026: files released by the US Justice Department included 2003 emails between Casey Wasserman and Ghislaine Maxwell, an associate of Jeffrey Epstein, with suggestive remarks. He said he deeply regrets them, that they came before her crimes were known, and that he had no personal or business relationship with Epstein.
https://frontofficesports.com/?p=222815
He has not been accused of any illegal activity in connection with the documents.
https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/theteam-forms-11-member-board-after-providence-completes-buyout-of-founder-casey-wasserman/

Clients left, mostly in music: singer Chappell Roan and about 20 other acts. In sports, soccer star Abby Wambach is the only athlete named as leaving; by May the sports business was reported to be running largely as normal.
https://frontofficesports.com/?p=235029
He stepped back in February, the name changed in March, and he sold his stake (about 40%) in July.
https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/casey-wasserman-sells-stake-the-team-providence-equity-1236658638/

Japanese players: no Japanese athlete was found to have left (searched twice, 21 Nov 2026). A Japanese weekly speculated in March that Wolfe might go independent or join a rival; that has not happened as far as reports show.
https://www.dailyshincho.jp/article/2026/03111001/?all=1
Casey Wasserman has chaired LA28, the organising committee, since 2017. This is his personal role; the agency does not run the Games.
https://la28.org/en/about-la28.html

11 Feb 2026: after a review by an outside law firm, LA28's executive committee kept him as chair. About a week later Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass called for him to resign, as did several county and city officials. In June he said he would not.
https://frontofficesports.com/?p=222815
The International Olympic Committee's coordination chief expressed 'full trust' in LA28's leadership; the IOC president said it would not involve itself in the committee's structure.
https://www.aol.com/news/ioc-continues-full-trust-casey-194412625.html
He was still speaking as LA28 chairperson on 19 Nov 2026.
https://coliseum-online.com/kennedy-appointed-as-head-of-ceremonies-and-content-for-la28
Since the 2026 sale he no longer owns the agency, so the old overlap (one man leading both the Games and an agency full of Olympic athletes) has ended.
https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/theteam-forms-11-member-board-after-providence-completes-buyout-of-founder-casey-wasserman/
Baseball is in the 2028 Games: six teams at Dodger Stadium. Japan is expected to qualify through the Premier12 tournament in November 2027.
https://thescore.com/mlb/news/3566495

Will MLB stars such as Ohtani and Yamamoto play? Not decided. As of July 2026 the owners support it, but the league and the players' union had no agreement (the dispute includes whether taking part is compulsory, insurance and scheduling). Nothing newer was found.
https://frontofficesports.com/article/la28-mlb-plan-remains-unsettled/
The agency represents Olympic athletes (swimmer Katie Ledecky is one). No contract between the agency and LA28, and no documented conflict of interest, was found.
https://frontofficesports.com/?p=222815

sections.title: Can it dominate in the future? (my analysis)

rows: For: the client chain in Japanese baseball is hard to copy, and every new star arrives already knowing Wolfe's name.
For: an owner that says it will keep funding growth and more purchases.
https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/casey-wasserman-providence-equity-taking-full-control-of-theteam/
For: scale. It is already No. 2 in the world, and the sports side lost almost no athletes in the 2026 crisis.
https://frontofficesports.com/?p=235029
Against: the business depends on a few people. When Tellem left in 2015 the link to Nomura went with him. If Wolfe left, the Japanese clients could follow him.
Against: strong rivals hold the other stars. Ohtani is with CAA's Nez Balelo; Scott Boras and Casey Close also sign Japanese players.
https://www.jiji.com/jc/v7?id=mlbjptoday

Against: the Japanese layer is getting stronger. Dentsu is reported around Yamamoto and Sasaki, and Hakuhodo bought Don Nomura's agency in 2025. If Japanese companies control the player at home, they can choose which American agent gets the job.
https://www.hakuhodo.co.jp/news/newsrelease/118591/
Against: an investment-firm owner usually wants to sell again in a few years, which can unsettle staff and clients.
A limit on who can ever buy it: investment firms that own shares in teams face a conflict if they also own a player agency. That kept several big bidders out in 2026.
https://frontofficesports.com/?p=235029
My reading: strong in Japanese baseball for now, but 'dominate' is too big a word. Power is shifting toward whoever holds the player's trust in Japan.
